4 1990s: Siesta time




Nešetřil’s 1989 paper [210] showed that all hereditary
Ramsey classes of freely ordered graphs had already been known earlier and concluded
with a conjecture that this is also the case for hereditary classes of freely ordered
hypergraphs. As a consequence of this, it seemed that the sources of potential candidates
for interesting Ramsey classes had run out, and in the 1990s the search for them has slowed
down. However, new candidates started emerging in the context of model theory, for which the 1990s
meant a significant progress.




4.1 Classification Programme of Homogeneous Structures




The celebrated (Cherlin and Lachlan’s) classification programme of homogeneous structures
aims to provide full catalogues of countable
homogeneous structures of a given type. The most important cases for structural Ramsey theory where the classification
is complete are:


1. 



Schmerl’s catalogue of homogeneous partial orders [265],


2. 



Lachlan and Woodrow’s catalogue of homogeneous (simple) graphs [196],


3. 



Lachlan’s catalogue of homogeneous tournaments [182],


4. 



Cherlin’s catalogue of homogeneous digraphs [63] (this generalizes catalogues 1, 2 and 3),


5. 



Cherlin’s catalogue of homogeneous ordered graphs [66] (the first classification result motivated by structural Ramsey theory),


6. 



Braunfeld’s catalogue of homogeneous finite-dimensional (generalized) permutation structures [47], which has recently been shown to be complete by Braunfeld and Simon [46, 49], and


7. 



Cherlin’s catalogue of metrically homogeneous graphs [66]. A proof of its completeness has been announced by Cherlin.

Conjecture 6.36 (Bodirsky–Pinsker, 2011; See [43]).



Let 𝐌\mathbf{M} be a first-order reduct of a finitely bounded homogeneous structure in a finite relational language. Then either CSP over 𝐌\mathbf{M} is solvable in polynomial time, or it is NP-complete.





Note that this in particular captures all finite structures. See [38] for more details.




The method of canonical functions (see e. g. [40] for details) was developed with the goal of verifying Conjecture 6.36 for first-order reducts of concrete homogeneous structures, and it has succeeded in several instances [24, 33, 41, 52, 172]. However, as an intermediate step, one has to classify all first-order reducts of the given structure (see Section 6.4.1), which tends to be very laborious. Recently, Mottet and Pinsker [205] introduced a powerful method of smooth approximations which is often able to circumvent this laborious step. Nevertheless, it still uses canonical functions and thus also Ramsey expansions. Consequently, the present methods are only able to say something about the following weakening of Conjecture 6.36:


Let 𝐌\mathbf{M} be a first-order reduct of a finitely bounded Ramsey structure in a finite relational language. Then either CSP over 𝐌\mathbf{M} is solvable in polynomial time, or it is NP-complete.


This was in fact the motivation behind Question 6.2, as well as the following conjecture:



Conjecture 6.37 (Bodirsky [38, Conjecture 11.1.1]).



Every finitely bounded homogeneous structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion.

6.4.1 Reducts of homogeneous structures




It is well-known that a permutation group GG is a closed subgroup of Sym(ℕ)\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits(\mathbb{N}) if and only if it is the automorphism group of some relational structure with vertex set ℕ\mathbb{N}. One can show that a countable structure 𝐌−\mathbf{M}^{-} is a first-order reduct of a structure 𝐌\mathbf{M} if and only if Aut(𝐌−)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}\nolimits(\mathbf{M}^{-}) is a closed supergroup of Aut(𝐌)\mathop{\mathrm{Aut}}\nolimits(\mathbf{M}), both seen as closed subgroups of Sym(M)\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits(M).
